items.text: Concept 5 · Inequalities

items.quote: Prove that algebraic inequalities are correct in various math situations (conditional).
items.text: Learning Outcomes: Prove that algebraic inequalities are correct in various math situations (conditional).

items.quote: You are a bio-engineer designing a biodegradable capsule
items.text: You are a bio-engineer designing a biodegradable capsule to deliver a life-saving drug to a specific tumour inside the human body. To ensure the drug releases at the perfect rate, you need the capsule to have the maximum possible volume, but you have a strict limit on the amount of expensive raw polymer available to create its outer surface area.

items.caption: Illustration of a capsule with labels: 'Exact mathematical equation', 'Single Equation', 'Specific Case: V=f(S) Traditional equation' (crossed out in a panel), 'VOLUME (to maximize)', 'LIFE-SAVING DRUG', 'SURFACE AREA (limited raw polymer)', and a small crossed-out capsule labelled 'Specific Case: V=f(S)'.
items.notes: Illustrative picture referred to by the text; labels read from image.

items.quote: How do you find the absolute best design when you can't
items.text: How do you find the absolute best design when you can't just use an exact equation to give you a single answer? You use inequalities. While regular equations tell us exactly when things are equal, inequalities tell us the optimal limits of what is physically possible—the absolute maximums and minimums. In life sciences, economics, and logistics, the most powerful tool for finding these bounds is a beautiful, universal mathematical law known as the AM-GM Inequality.

items.quote: How can algebraic techniques and the structural properties of positive real numbers
items.text: Guiding question: How can algebraic techniques and the structural properties of positive real numbers be used to establish definitive upper and lower bounds for variable expressions, and how does equality emerge as a special boundary condition?

items.quote: To prove inequalities with radicals, calculate the difference of their squares
items.claim: To prove inequalities with radicals, calculate the difference of their squares, (LHS)^2 − (RHS)^2.
When LHS > 0 and RHS > 0: (LHS)^2 > (RHS)^2 if and only if LHS > RHS.
(LHS)^2 ≥ (RHS)^2 if and only if LHS ≥ RHS (under the same condition LHS>0, RHS>0).
items.notes: Printed as continuation line of the first bullet, without its own bullet.

items.stem: Prove that if a > 0 and b > 0, √((a²+b²)/2) ≥ (a+b)/2, and determine when equality holds (Warm Up 1).
solution: Since a > 0, b > 0, $\sqrt{\frac{a^2+b^2}{2}}>0$, $\frac{a+b}{2}>0$ ...(ii) (side note: Must show LHS > 0, RHS > 0)
From (i) and (ii), $\sqrt{\frac{a^2+b^2}{2}}\ge\frac{a+b}{2}$ (side note: Proved LHS ≥ RHS)
Also, equality holds when $\frac{a-b}{2}=0$, that is, when $a=b$. (side note: Equality holds when X = 0)
items.notes: Printed as '1 [Proof]' under Explanation; stem inferred from Warm Up 1. Side notes printed in right column.

Proving Inequalities (4) (AM-GM Inequality)

items.quote: Applies the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality to prove inequalities

items.quote: The AM-GM inequality is highly useful when the product of the terms simplifies to a constant.
items.claim: The AM-GM inequality is highly useful when the product of the terms simplifies to a constant. Example: a + 1/a ⇒ a × 1/a = 1.

items.text: Reflect

items.quote: We proved in the lesson that the AM-GM Inequality
items.text: We proved in the lesson that the AM-GM Inequality ($\frac{a+b}{2} \ge \sqrt{ab}$) always holds true, provided that the numbers are non-negative ($a, b \ge 0$).

items.quote: What happens if we try to break this condition
items.text: What happens if we try to break this condition and apply the inequality to negative numbers? Suppose that $a = -2$ and $b = -8$.
Calculate their Arithmetic Mean (AM).

items.quote: Attempt to calculate their Geometric Mean (GM).
items.text: Attempt to calculate their Geometric Mean (GM).

items.quote: Does the inequality sign (≥) still hold true
items.text: Does the inequality sign ($\ge$) still hold true and remain valid?

items.quote: Explain the algebraic and logical breakdown that occurs here
items.text: Explain the algebraic and logical breakdown that occurs here, and why defining “domains and restrictions” in inequalities is vital to prevent medical and engineering models from collapsing in the real world.

learning_objectives.label: Prove conditional inequalities
learning_objectives.description: Prove a conditional inequality by calculating LHS − RHS, factorising it and using the given conditions (e.g. a > b rewritten as a − b > 0) to show the result is positive.

learning_objectives.label: Prove by completing the square
learning_objectives.description: Prove an inequality for all real numbers by completing the square to form X² or X² + Y², and determine when equality holds.

learning_objectives.label: Prove inequalities with roots
learning_objectives.description: Prove inequalities containing square roots by calculating (LHS)² − (RHS)², showing LHS > 0 and RHS > 0, and determine when equality holds.

learning_objectives.label: Apply the AM-GM inequality
learning_objectives.description: Apply the AM-GM inequality for positive a and b to prove inequalities, determine when equality holds (a = b), and find maximum values such as an area.
